Yes—there are real disconnects in the current implementation. The main issue is that **settings, push routing, checkpoint reads, `status`, and `doctor` do not share one complete destination resolver**.

I inspected the checkout and merged history without changing files or pushing anything.

One important caveat: your installed CLI is `0.10.1-nightly.202608180612.e2de3d346` from August 18, while this checkout is from August 25 and contains later fixes. Its live output is therefore not a reliable test of this checkout.

### How remote selection currently works

Two similarly named settings control different things:

| Setting under `strategy_options` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"checkpoint_push_remote": "upstream"` | Choose a configured Git remote that carries checkpoints. |
| `"checkpoint_remote": {"provider":"github","repo":"org/checkpoints"}` | Route checkpoints to a separate repository using a derived URL. |
| `"push_sessions": false` | Disable automatic checkpoint pushes. |

The local settings layer overrides project settings **by strategy-option key**. A local `checkpoint_remote` replaces that whole object.

For ordinary named remotes, selection follows:

1. Explicit `checkpoint_push_remote`.
2. A previously observed and saved checkpoint destination.
3. `origin`.
4. The sole remote, or the first configured remote.

An explicit nonexistent remote disables checkpoint syncing. A push to another remote normally sends code without checkpoints. Automatic selection can move after a qualifying push delivers checkpoints, but it does not follow every subsequent branch or push.

Crucially, setting `checkpoint_push_remote` does **not** mean “whenever I push code anywhere, separately push checkpoints to this remote.” It determines which code pushes are allowed to carry checkpoints.

A successfully resolved **dedicated `checkpoint_remote` bypasses that restriction**. See [checkpoint_sync_remote.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go:43).

### Where the behavior disconnects

**1. A configured dedicated repository can deliberately be ignored.**

For a `checkpoint_remote` in tracked `settings.json`, the current ownership guard checks both `origin` and every push URL. An owner mismatch—or an owner it cannot determine—makes the setting look inherited from upstream.

That disables dedicated routing for that push; the normal single-remote gate then applies. Putting the setting in an untracked `settings.local.json` establishes explicit local intent and bypasses the ownership heuristic.

This explains how a valid setting can appear “not respected.” It is an intentional heuristic, but it also affects legitimate backups or repositories under another organization.

**2. Writes can reject that setting while reads still use it.**

The fetch resolver does not apply the same ownership check. Consequently, writes may go to an elected remote while reads look in the configured dedicated repository.

The commit introducing the latest ownership restriction explicitly calls this out as **“Not addressed.”** This is a confirmed code-path mismatch, although I have not reproduced your particular failure. See [util.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/remote/util.go:194).

**3. `status` predicts one destination, but pushes resolve against the actual push target.**

`status` probes dedicated routing using the elected remote. A push to another remote can produce a different ownership verdict.

It also reports a bad `checkpoint_push_remote` before checking the dedicated-repository exemption—even though the hook may successfully push to the dedicated repository. Both discrepancies are explicitly documented as “accepted divergence” in [status.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/status.go:320).

**4. The doctor destination warning describes topology, not the complete election.**

It examines all remotes and whether each resolves to a dedicated repository. It does not use `checkpoint_push_remote` to decide that an otherwise ambiguous topology has been explicitly resolved.

So the warning can remain after you have selected a checkpoint remote. Its advice also emphasizes `checkpoint_remote`, despite the named-remote setting being a different legitimate solution.

**5. Checkpoint refs are tracked for one delivery destination.**

The refs backend’s queue records refs without per-destination delivery state. For a remote with multiple push URLs, it pushes checkpoints to the **first URL only**. The older branch backend retains Git’s fan-out behavior.

That also means an empty queue is not proof that checkpoints exist on every remote—or on a newly selected destination.

| [#1897](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1897), [#1905](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1905) | Multi-push-URL tests, first-destination refs pushes, and destination warnings. |

| [#1951](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1951) | Reads follow the elected remote, with origin as a legacy read fallback. |

[#2327](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2327) directly addresses several issues we identified. It is currently **open, not merged**.

It adds three substantial changes:

- **Correct configuration advice:** doctor and multi-URL warnings now distinguish `checkpoint_push_remote` (a remote name) from `checkpoint_remote` (a dedicated repository object).
- **Automatic Entire destination:** a single qualifying `entire://` remote becomes preferred over `origin`. Every code push then sends checkpoints there, even when pushing code elsewhere.
- **Explicit backlog migration:** `entire checkpoint migrate` republishes existing checkpoints, verifies delivery, and optionally removes old copies with separate consent. Status gains migration reporting.

However, the diff reveals an important remaining inconsistency: **automatic selection and explicit configuration of the same Entire remote behave differently.**

| Selection of the Entire remote | Checkpoints accompany pushes to other remotes? |
|---|---|
| Automatically selected through the new `entire` tier | Yes |
| Explicit `checkpoint_push_remote` setting | No—the ordinary gate still applies |
| Previously captured destination | No—the ordinary gate still applies |

The redirect checks `elected.Source == SyncRemoteSourceEntire`, rather than whether the selected destination is an Entire remote. Explicit settings outrank that tier and return source `config`. Consequently, explicitly selecting the destination can disable the behavior automatic selection provides. Doctor’s new “destination settled” handling also only recognizes source `entire`. [Relevant diff](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2327/files)

Two other limitations matter for your setup:

- Your `origin` has a GitHub fetch URL and an `entire://` push URL. The new detection requires **every fetch and push URL** to be `entire://`, so that mixed remote does not qualify.
- Successfully resolved dedicated `checkpoint_remote` routing still takes precedence. This PR does not unify its ownership checks, read routing, and status prediction.

So this is highly relevant work, particularly for misleading advice and stranded historical checkpoints. But it also gives us a concrete case to investigate next: **why explicitly choosing a remote changes delivery semantics compared with automatically choosing that exact same remote.** This conclusion is from inspecting the diff; I haven’t run its tests.

The screenshots confirm the failure chain: **the CLI’s advice led the user to an invalid configuration.**

`remote_wrong.png` tells them to set `checkpoint_remote` in `.entire/settings.json`, without showing its structure. They reasonably added:

```json
"checkpoint_remote": "entire"
```

`settings_remote.png` shows that at the top level. There are two problems:

- **Wrong location:** the settings parser rejects unknown top-level fields, causing `entire status` to fail entirely.
- **Wrong setting:** choosing the Git remote named `entire` requires `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`. Merely moving `"checkpoint_remote": "entire"` under `strategy_options` would stop that parsing error but silently ignore the string—it expects a repository object.

The correct configuration is to remove the invalid top-level entry, preserve their other project settings, and add this to `.entire/settings.local.json`:

```json
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "checkpoint_push_remote": "entire"
  }
}
```

Using the local file keeps a clone-specific remote name out of teammates’ configuration. The setting also works under `strategy_options` in project `settings.json`; that file itself is not the cause of the error.

This strengthens the case for #2327’s wording fix, but we should also cover **recovery from the already-broken configuration**. Better advice alone will not repair those files. The parser should ideally explain the correct key and nesting when it encounters this particular mistake.

And the earlier #2327 concern applies directly here: explicitly setting `"checkpoint_push_remote": "entire"` selects source `config`, so the proposed automatic Entire redirect does not apply. Pushing to `entire` can carry checkpoints; pushing code to `origin` still skips them. That needs to be reconciled with the intended behavior.

- Explicitly setting `checkpoint_push_remote: "entire"` bypasses the new automatic tier, so pushes to `origin` still won’t send checkpoints to `entire`.

okay so what else needs fixing?

Beyond #2327’s wording fix, I’d prioritize these:

1. **Make explicit and automatic selection behave consistently.** In #2327, automatically selecting an Entire remote sends checkpoints there on every code push. Explicitly selecting that same remote with `checkpoint_push_remote` disables that redirect. This is the clearest remaining behavior issue.

They need a shared resolution result, including why a setting was ignored.

3. **Make configuration errors actionable.** Top-level `checkpoint_remote` should explain the required nesting. A string under `strategy_options.checkpoint_remote` should produce a clear validation error instead of being silently ignored. Already-broken files need useful recovery guidance.

4. **Handle destination changes and historical checkpoints consistently.** Changing the selected remote does not republish refs already removed from the push queue. #2327 adds migration, but status should distinguish “nothing queued” from “all checkpoints verified at this destination,” including explicitly selected destinations.

5. **Clarify mixed fetch/push URL support.** Your GitHub-fetch / Entire-push `origin` does not qualify for #2327’s automatic Entire tier. We should establish the intended behavior for that common setup and make the reporting match it.

okay how would we do 2?

I’d introduce one shared **checkpoint routing resolver**, then make push, reads, `status`, and `doctor` consume its result.

Today, the named-remote election and dedicated-repository resolution happen separately, with callers deciding precedence and fallback behavior. That’s where they disagree.

The resolver should return:

- The configured destination and which setting selected it.
- The effective write destination.
- Whether syncing is enabled, disabled, or waiting for a push to the selected remote.
- Why a dedicated setting was rejected or could not resolve.
- Read destinations, distinguishing the active store from historical fallbacks.

There’s one important distinction to preserve: **status describes configuration; the hook evaluates a specific push.** We shouldn’t make status guess which remote the next push will target. They should share the same rules, with the hook supplying the actual push target.

For example, status could say:

```text
Checkpoints: upstream (set by checkpoint_push_remote)
Syncs when pushing to upstream.
Dedicated repository org/checkpoints ignored: ownership mismatch.
```

Then I’d update the consumers:

| Consumer | Change |
|---|---|
| Push hook | Use the resolved destination and eligibility directly. |
| Reads | Look in the effective checkpoint store first; retain appropriate historical fallbacks. |
| Status | Show the selection, conditions, and rejection reasons. Keep it network-free. |
| Doctor | Diagnose unresolved configuration; stop treating multiple remotes alone as ambiguity. |

The tricky case is ownership rejection: if writes go to a fork, reads should search that fork first. The inherited dedicated repository might still contain useful upstream history, so I wouldn’t simply remove it from all reads—but it must not remain the assumed authoritative write destination.

I’d implement this in two stages:

1. Extract the shared resolution without changing behavior.
2. Correct the disagreements with focused regression tests: ownership mismatch, explicit non-origin selection, invalid named remote alongside a dedicated repository, and different fetch/push URLs.

That can start independently of #2327. Its Entire redirect would then become another explicit rule in the shared resolver, rather than a separate exception each command has to understand.

| Case | What happens | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| `push_sessions: false` | Status still says “Checkpoints sync to: upstream.” The hook skips automatic checkpoint pushes. | Status checks whether Entire is enabled, but never checks whether checkpoint pushing is disabled. |

| Different fetch and push URLs | Reads and writes can reach different repositories while status displays the same remote name. | Readers resolve the fetch URL; writers use push URLs. The remote name hides that distinction. |

### The most consequential call-site mismatch

For a configuration with:

```text
origin: acme/app
fork: contributor/app
checkpoint_push_remote: fork
checkpoint_remote: acme/checkpoints
```

The paths disagree:

- **Push:** `prePush` → `resolvePushSettings` → `PushURL` rejects the dedicated repository on ownership grounds → the election permits `fork`.

- **Blob hydration:** `checkpointBlobFetchTargets` likewise selects only the dedicated target.
